one_liner: Rust async gRPC (tokio, hyper, prost) that out-served the stock C++ gRPC async servers in grpc_bench's small unary echo test.
what_it_does: tonic is a gRPC client and server library for Rust: tonic-build or tonic-prost-build generates async service traits and client stubs from .proto files, and you implement each RPC as an async method taking &self and a Request<T>. It supports unary and bi-directional streaming RPCs, TLS through rustls, load balancing, custom metadata, health checking and reflection, and it interoperates on the wire with any other gRPC implementation. It is a different API, not a drop-in for grpc++: a C++ program reaches it only through a separate process or an FFI bridge.
how_it_is_fast: The README describes three layers: a generic gRPC core, the hyper/h2 HTTP/2 implementation on tokio, and prost codegen, all compiled together, so the grpc_bench build gets whole-program opt-level 3, LTO and codegen-units 1 plus jemalloc. The winning 1-CPU variant, rust_tonic_st, runs tokio's current_thread runtime: one event loop with no cross-thread wake-ups or work stealing. That last point is the benchmark's setup rather than a documented tonic technique. Part of the measured gap comes from the C++ side, not from tonic (see gotchas).
when_to_use: New gRPC services or clients written in Rust: async/await on tokio, prost-generated types, streaming, rustls TLS, health and reflection services.

Small unary RPCs at high concurrency in CPU-capped containers. In grpc_bench's 1-CPU complex_proto test, rust_tonic_st served 41,546 req/s against 24,926-26,700 for the three C++ servers in 2022, and 102,754 against 56,669-57,403 in the 2026-04-23 run.
One process per core with predictable tails: the current_thread variant held p99 at 33.24 ms (2022) and 14.47 ms (2026) at 1 CPU, while the multi-thread runtime's p99 was 668.38 ms and 98.22 ms.
Memory-tight sidecars: 12-18 MiB average memory in grpc_bench, close to the C++ servers (about 9-37 MiB) and far below dotnet_grpc (114-176 MiB).
when_not_to_use: In-process use from C++. Tuning grpc++ (more pre-registered requests per completion queue, or the callback API) is likely cheaper than adding a Rust process, and the grpc_bench C++ baseline never did that tuning.

Multi-core servers judged on the 2022 data alone. At 2 and 3 CPUs, cpp_grpc_mt (69,882 and 71,806 req/s) and cpp_asio_grpc beat rust_tonic_mt (53,832 and 64,091). tonic_mt led C++ at 2-4 CPUs only in the 2026 run.
The multi-thread runtime under a 1-CPU quota when tail latency matters: p99 was about 20x (2022) and 7x (2026) worse than the current_thread variant.

When you need a stable API: the crate is still 0.x, master is preparing breaking changes (the README points to the 0.14.x branch), and the repository now lives at grpc/grpc-rust next to a new grpc crate.
Tail-latency-critical clients on aarch64: issue #1606 (elevated p99 and above on a master client compared with v0.10.2) is still open and has no root cause.

integration.dependencies: tokio, hyper 1 and h2 0.4, hyper-util, tower 0.5, axum 0.8 (default router feature), bytes, tokio-stream, tokio-util; prost through tonic-prost; optional rustls (tls-ring or tls-aws-lc), flate2 (gzip/deflate), zstd; codegen in tonic-build/tonic-prost-build needs protoc
integration.min_toolchain: Rust 1.88 (MSRV in the README and the workspace rust-version); the 2022 benchmark used Rust 1.59 with tonic 0.7
integration.platforms: not documented in the README (any target tokio supports); grpc_bench measured only x86-64 Linux in Docker
integration.thread_safety: Handlers take &self and may run concurrently on a multi-thread tokio runtime, so shared service state needs Sync types; the README documents no other threading rules.
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — wire-compatible with gRPC C++ peers (the repo carries interop tests), but a different language and API; C++ code cannot link it as a grpc++ replacement

gotchas: Harness flaw in the baseline: all three grpc_bench C++ servers (cpp_grpc_st, cpp_grpc_mt and cpp_asio_grpc) post exactly one RequestSayHello per completion queue, while the client keeps 1000 requests in flight. In the CallData servers, each call registers its successor only on reaching PROCESS. The asio-grpc server runs one accept-loop coroutine per GrpcContext and awaits one agrpc::request at a time. gRPC's own performance guide says to 'register enough server requests for the desired level of concurrency' to avoid 'a slow path that results in essentially serial request processing'. grpc_bench issue #490 (opened 2024-11-04, still open) reports this for cpp_grpc_mt; the maintainer replied that the code came from the gRPC examples. The server code is unchanged at the 2026 run's commit c4c93b3. The C++ servers also link the distro libgrpc++ package, asio-grpc is pinned to 1.0.0, and cpp_grpc_mt runs one thread per completion queue, where the guide (as of gRPC 1.41) suggests two. So the C++ numbers are a lower bound for grpc++, which is consistent with rust_grpcio (C core) also beating them at 1 CPU (31,035 req/s in 2022).

The record's caveat that the win appears only at 1 CPU is outdated. In the 2026-04-23 run (discussion #559, Xeon Gold 6548N, 4096m server RAM, tonic 0.14 on Rust 1.94), rust_tonic_mt beat the best C++ server at 2, 3 and 4 CPUs: 130,370 vs 74,869 (1.74x), 139,886 vs 81,581 (1.71x) and 136,638 vs 85,485 (1.60x), derived from page data. The same under-registered C++ harness was used.

Results depend on the runtime flavour. At 1 CPU, current_thread beat multi-thread by 17-25% in throughput and by 7-20x at p99. A current_thread server uses one core per process, so scaling out means several processes behind SO_REUSEPORT or a load balancer.

Tonic was not alone. At 1 CPU in 2022, go_vtgrpc (44,074) and rust_thruster_st (41,334) matched or beat rust_tonic_st, and in 2026 dotnet_grpc reached 84,809 against 57,403 for the best C++ server. The lead over C++ is a property of this harness as much as of tonic.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick tonic over Thruster (thruster-grpc) when you want the mainstream Rust gRPC stack with prost codegen, TLS, health, reflection and xDS work; rust_thruster_st was within 0.5-4.2% of rust_tonic_st in both grpc_bench runs (41,334 vs 41,546 and 98,464 vs 102,754). Pick it over grpc-dotnet or grpc-go when the service is in Rust or memory is tight (about 13-15 MiB vs 120-135 MiB for dotnet_grpc in 2026); grpc-dotnet was close in multi-core throughput (136,452 vs 139,886 at 3 CPUs).
verified_claims_summary: In grpc_bench's complex_proto unary echo test (commit 14a8435, 2022-04-23 wiki page, Xeon E5-1650 v3, 50 connections, 1000 in-flight requests, 120 s after a 30 s warm-up), rust_tonic_st (tonic 0.7, Rust 1.59, LTO, jemalloc) served 41,546 req/s at 1 CPU. The C++ servers, built with g++ 11 -O3 -flto against the distro libgrpc++, served 26,700 (cpp_grpc_st), 26,376 (cpp_grpc_mt) and 24,926 (cpp_asio_grpc), so tonic was 1.56-1.67x faster, but cpp_grpc_mt led at 2 and 3 CPUs. All three C++ servers register only one pending request per completion queue, which gRPC's performance guide warns serialises request handling.
status_note: Actively maintained: last commit 2026-10-07, MIT, 12.5k stars. The project now lives at github.com/grpc/grpc-rust (hyperium/tonic redirects there), and the latest release is the 0.14.x line, with breaking changes pending on master. It is a copyable crate, but the measured advantage over C++ rests on an untuned grpc++ harness: one outstanding request per completion queue, the open grpc_bench issue #490.
